<reason>A close, high-level debate. A held the textual high ground: the standards/terms split and the natural reading of "basic terms" were strong, and A landed an early concession-catch (B defends no bans and accepts "harmonize later"). A's pressure questions were excellent and forced B to supply finish lines. But B answered the debate's hardest pressure—A's Q1 demanding a specific post-approval rule conventional meat escapes—with three concrete obligations unified by a temporal-hazard principle, then defended that answer when A's closing tried to equate it with the existing regime, dismantling the equation rule-by-rule with the drift/template distinction. B's Rebuttal 2 was the standout turn: direct A1/A2 answers plus the voluntary-vs-mandatory label turn, leaving A's parity visibly shrunken toward "regulated as food," which fed B's emptiness critique of the motion's operative phrase. A's clipped opening was a minor added execution cost. B's edge is real but narrow because A's motion-faithful reading and the unanswered COOL/"previously frozen" mandatory-label counter kept A's route alive to the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange ran A3.1 (Q1: name one post-approval rule conventional meat escapes and the hazard pre-market review can't address) → B4.1 (three rules: ongoing genomic drift verification, batch-level media-residue screening, long-latency surveillance—each a hazard that only exists after approval) → A5.1-5.2 ("you just described the existing meat regime") → B5.1's rule-by-rule dismantling ("no steer is re-sequenced against a dossier, because a steer cannot drift"; "a steak cannot become something else in the tank"). B answered the hardest question squarely and then defended the answer under attack—the point where "same basic terms" took the most damage.</best_rebuttal>
